chapters.summary: Councilmember Pierina Sanchez identifies herself as chair and announces the committee will vote on Proposed Intro 905-A, the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act. She notes the bill is sponsored by Councilmember Sandy Nurse and concerns qualified entities' first opportunity to submit a statement of interest and purchase certain properties.
chapters.title: Chair Sanchez opens vote on COPA Intro 905-A

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Pierina Sanchez, Chair of the Committee on Housing and Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Today, the committee will be voting on Proposed Intro 905A, the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, sponsored by Councilmember Sandy Nurse, in relation to giving qualified entities a first opportunity to submit a statement of interest.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And the first opportunity to purchase certain properties.

chapters.summary: Sanchez says New York City faces a profound housing crisis beyond the need to build more, pointing to failing infrastructure, dangerous conditions, and buildings trapped in speculation, disinvestment, and neglect. She argues the city cannot build its way out while existing affordable housing falls apart.
chapters.title: Sanchez frames COPA as response to deteriorating housing stock

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: New York City is in a profound housing crisis, and while we rightly talk about our desperate need to build more, we cannot ignore another crisis that is unfolding inside the homes we already have, the deterioration of our existing housing stock.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Across our city, tenants are living with failing infrastructure, dangerous conditions, and buildings caught in cycles of speculation, disinvestment, and neglect.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Our city cannot build our way out of this crisis while allowing the affordable housing that we already have to fall apart.

chapters.summary: Sanchez describes COPA as a tool to interrupt speculative cycles by giving mission-driven organizations a chance when buildings change hands. She explains that covered 4-to-100-unit buildings with HPD affordability agreements or physical distress would require owners to notify qualified entities, allow offers, and let a qualified entity match later private offers.
chapters.title: Sanchez explains COPA notice, offer, and match process

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And that's why today's vote is so exciting, because with COPA, New York City gains a new tool to interrupt those cycles and put buildings on a path toward long-term stability and responsible ownership.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Championed by Councilmember Sandy Nurse and heard by this committee several times, COPA recognizes that the moment a building changes hands is a critical opportunity to change its future

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: by giving mission-driven organizations a meaningful chance to acquire the buildings and chart a different, non-speculative future for families who live there.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: 905 would require that if owners of a select group of multifamily residential buildings decide to sell those properties, they must offer these buildings to select nonprofits

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: called qualified entities before they can complete the sale of those buildings to a private party.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: COPA would include buildings with between 4 and 100 units that either have

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: affordability agreements managed by HPD or have a baseline level of physical distress.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: HPD would manage a list of qualified entities who are experienced operators of residential buildings and owners of covered buildings would be required first to notify these entities before they complete a sale,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: then to give those entities a period of time to make an offer to purchase the building.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: If the building owner rejects any offers from a qualified entity, that qualified entity would be given the opportunity to match any offers that the owner later receives from private sellers.

chapters.summary: Sanchez says COPA is inspired by a San Francisco program that helped prevent displacement of thousands of tenants. She argues nonprofits need time to assemble financing and can better maintain lower rents, especially as affordability agreements expire and vacancy rates for low-rent apartments are extremely low.
chapters.title: Sanchez cites San Francisco model and nonprofit financing barriers

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: This program is inspired by a similar program in San Francisco that has helped prevent the displacement of thousands of tenants.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It would help mission-oriented nonprofits compete with speculative investors to acquire housing and enable them to maintain the city's affordable housing stock.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Tens of thousands of regulatory agreements requiring developers to maintain affordable rents in New York expire every year.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The vacancy rate for apartments with rents below $1,100 is estimated at just 0.39%.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: It is below 1% for apartments with rents under $1,649.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: The city doesn't have enough affordable housing to spare, and we must do what we can to keep those affordability agreements alive.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Nonprofits have been shown to be more effective at maintaining lower rents, but they can't give legitimate offers to purchase property at the same rate as speculative investors.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: They rely too heavily on a bundle of...

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: financing from across many sources.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: COPA would give these nonprofits the time they need to purchase residential buildings, preventing the displacement of tenants that call those buildings their home, and enabling these nonprofits to maintain New York's affordable housing stock.

chapters.summary: Sanchez recognizes Councilmember Sandy Nurse for pouring labor, political capital, and patience into the legislation. She also credits the COPA Coalition, led by the New Economy Project and including tenant leaders, before inviting Nurse to discuss her bill.
chapters.title: Sanchez thanks Nurse and COPA Coalition before inviting sponsor

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I want to especially recognize Councilmember Sandy Nurse, who's poured so much labor, political capital, and patience.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Girl.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Into getting this legislation across the finish line.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I also want to recognize the tireless advocacy of the COPA Coalition, led by the New Economy Project, nicely, including so many organizations and tenant leaders, shout out to our Bronx from my neck of the woods, who have been fighting for this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd like to invite Councilmember Nurse now to discuss her bill.

chapters.summary: Nurse thanks Chair Sanchez and says the vote ends a six-year saga involving three mayors, four introductions, three hearings, a passage and veto, and intense real estate lobbying. She says the committee is voting on the most strategic and operationally sound version, crediting the COPA Coalition and colleagues' input.
chapters.title: Nurse recounts six-year COPA fight and revised bill

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Colleagues, today we are going to end the six-year saga of the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act here in the Council.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Three mayors, four introductions, three hearings, a passage and a veto, a really intense lobbying effort by the real estate industry, all of it.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Comes down to today's vote.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We are voting on the most strategic, most operationally sound version of this bill, thanks to the relentless campaign of the COPA Coalition and also to the invaluable input of many of my colleagues here.

chapters.summary: Nurse says COPA lets trusted housing providers buy certain buildings, work with tenants, fix units, and keep the same tenants at permanently affordable rates. She argues building alone cannot solve the crisis, cites New Yorkers planning to leave over cost, and says COPA gives community-oriented buyers public oversight.
chapters.title: Nurse presents COPA as anti-displacement and preservation tool

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: COPA lets trusted housing providers by certain buildings work with tenants,

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: fix these units up, and put those

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: same tenants back in those units at permanently affordable rates.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It is a critical anti-displacement tool.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And as one in five New Yorkers say they plan to leave within five years because it costs too damn much to stay, we can offer a chance.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We can't only build our way out of this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: If we are serious about stopping displacement, buying and preserving some of the existing housing stock has to be a priority.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And that's what COPA does.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: When a building is at risk, the people who live there and the surrounding community can get a real chance to fight for it.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It gives eligible landlords a pool of community-oriented buyers who know this work and know how to do it, and it brings these buildings under public oversight.

chapters.summary: Nurse promises a longer list of thanks later but singles out the New York City Community Land Initiative for disciplined, collaborative work that persisted through roadblocks and a veto. She thanks Progressive Caucus allies and members who opposed the bill for hearing her out, then asks for an aye vote.
chapters.title: Nurse thanks Community Land Initiative and colleagues, asks for vote

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: There are a ton of groups to name and thank.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I'll do all of that later to the annoyance of the majority leader.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: But the New York City Community Land Initiative has really, really done so much work here.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And I'm just so impressed with how disciplined and unrelenting they have been, how collaborative they've been.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And they haven't let any roadblocks, vetoes, or setbacks to stop them.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And I just really want to thank my colleagues who championed this bill, the Progressive Caucus especially, but also those who have been against this bill.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I really appreciate you patiently hearing me out and letting me bug you.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Even if you vote no, I really, really value that you gave me some time to hear me out.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Because this bill has really been through the fire, it is why I believe it is the best version that we could be voting on.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It is a program that I believe this council is going to be able to stand behind in the coming years.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So I ask for your vote, and thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Sanchez thanks Nurse and her own team, including Deputy Chiefs of Staff Ben Ratner and Kim Castellanos, District Director Maria Jose Mares, and other staff. She also thanks Housing and Buildings Committee staff and lists members present before asking the clerk to call the roll.
chapters.title: Sanchez thanks staff and calls roll call

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Nurse, and congratulations.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd like to also thank my team, Deputy Chiefs of Staff Ben Ratner and Kim Castellanos, District Director Maria Jose Mares, Gerard Fernandez, Soraya Bonilla, Oriana Roa Acevedo, Malia Sardinia, and Marcus Khan.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'd also like to thank the Housing and Buildings Committee staff, Senior Legislative Council Austin Malone,

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Legislative Council Billy X, Senior Policy Analyst Jose Conde, Senior Policy Analyst Dirk Spencer, Data Scientist Mohamed Shadid and Noah Slosberg, and Finance Analyst Carla Naranjo and Spencer Kuhn.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm joined today by the members of our committee, including Deputy Speaker Williams, Majority Leader Abreu, Council Members Wilson, Maloney, Salam, Riley, Felice, Hudson, Joseph, and Zhuang.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And with that, I will now ask the clerk to call the roll.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Rita C. Joseph asks to explain her vote and recalls telling District 40 tenants in January that the COPA fight was not over. She describes no-heat, mold, and repair complaints in Flatbush, Prospect Lefferts Gardens, Ditmas Park, and Crown Heights, arguing COPA breaks the cycle of distressed buildings being sold to developers.
chapters.title: Joseph explains aye vote, citing District 40 housing conditions

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Permission to explain my vote?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In January, when COPA fell short, I told tenants of District 40 that the fight was not over.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Today, we keep that promise.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I want to thank Councilmember Nurse to never backing down for years of negotiating, listening, and refusing to let this bill die.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you to the tenant organizers, the community land trust, and the advocates who kept showing up.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you to the speaker and the mayor for helping bring COPA home.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Let me tell you why this matter in Flatbush, Prospect, Lefferts Garden, Dittmas Park, and Crown Heights.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: My office take calls, no heat in January, molds in babies'bedrooms, ceilings coming down, repairs promised and never made.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Too many of my constituents live in buildings owned by landlords who treat their home as a line on a spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And when those buildings are sold, they are too often go to other developers and the cycle starts all over.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: COPA breaks that cycle.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: When a distressed building goes up for sale, mission-driven non-for-profits and community land trusts will finally get a fair first shot at buying it and keeping it affordable, safe, and in the hands of the community.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: As a forever educator for more than two decades, I learned that children cannot learn without a stable home.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And this is what is at stake for families in these buildings.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And this is why COPA matters.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Housing is not a commodity.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It is a home.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I proudly vote aye.

summary: The Committee on Housing and Buildings votes on Proposed Intro 905-A, the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act (COPA), after Chair Pierina Ana Sanchez and sponsor Sandy Nurse present the bill.

COPA would require owners of certain 4-to-100-unit multifamily buildings to notify and offer qualified nonprofit entities a first chance to purchase before a private sale, with a right to match later offers.
The committee approves the bill 10-0 with one abstention, as members praise Councilmember Nurse's six-year effort to pass COPA.
title: Committee on Housing and Buildings
topic: Giving qualified entities a first opportunity to submit a statement of interest and a first opportunity to purchase certain properties
